info.name: Relayed agent runtime
info.description:
The agent runtime's HTTP surface (docs/AGENT-RUNTIME.md §3).

Import this, set `agentKey` to whatever `AGENT_S2S_KEY` is in your `.env`, and the requests work against `pnpm agent` on :8788.

**Two things to know before you start.**

1. **A run is synchronous.** `POST /run` holds the connection until the loop finishes — that can be minutes. Postman's default request timeout is unlimited, but if you have set one in Settings → General, raise it or you will see a client-side timeout that looks like the service hanging.

2. **Streaming is the same endpoint.** `Accept: text/event-stream` selects it; anything else gets one JSON body. The `done` frame carries the JSON mode's body verbatim, so the two modes agree by construction. Postman renders the stream as raw text rather than parsing frames, which is enough to read it.

Variables: `baseUrl`, `agentKey`, `model` (leave empty to use the configured fallback), `runId` (captured automatically by the run requests).

variable.description: Must equal AGENT_S2S_KEY. Sent as x-agent-key.
Empty means the configured AGENT_MODEL_FALLBACK. Otherwise '<provider>/<model-id>', e.g. litellm/kimi-latest.
Captured from the last run. Used by the cancel request.

request.description: Answers as long as the process is up. Says nothing about capacity — use /healthz/ready for that.

200 with the in-flight count while accepting work; 503 once SIGTERM has started a drain. A draining process still finishes the runs it holds — readiness going red is how a load balancer stops sending it new ones.

The default mode: one JSON body when the loop finishes.

The prompt above deliberately exercises the tool palette — `write` then `read`, in the run's own disposable workspace — so a 200 with a non-empty `toolCalls` array proves more than the model merely answering.

**A run that started and failed is a 200 with `status: "failed"`.** Non-2xx is reserved for a bad request or an unavailable service. A failed run consumed tokens, may have run tools, and has a `runId` worth correlating; collapsing it into a 500 would throw that away.

`status: "completed"` with empty `text` is also a real outcome, not an error — it usually means the model said nothing after its last tool call.

pm.test('status is one of the four terminal states', () => {

// is the useful part of it.
console.log('run did not complete:', body.status, body.error ?? '(no reason given)');

request.description:
The same endpoint, selected by the `Accept` header rather than a body field — the body describes the run, the header describes how the answer travels.

Frames, in order:

- `started` — carries the `runId` immediately, which is what makes cancel usable
- `delta` — answer text, coalesced rather than one frame per token
- `reasoning` — thinking text, only when `AGENT_STREAM_REASONING=true`
- `tool` — `phase: start` then `phase: end` around each call
- `done` — the JSON mode's body, verbatim, under `result`

Every frame has a monotonic `seq` so a gap is detectable, a terminal `done` is always written before close (including on failure and during drain), and a `: keepalive` comment goes out every 25s so nothing in the middle idles the connection out.

Postman shows the raw stream rather than parsing frames. `curl -N` is the better tool if you want to watch it arrive.

exec: pm.test('opens with started and closes with done', () => {
// The runId arrives in the FIRST frame, before any model work — which
// is the whole reason cancel is usable against a stream and not against
// a JSON run that only answers once it is already over.
// The §3 contract: the done frame's result IS the JSON mode's body.
pm.test('done carries the same result shape as JSON mode', () => {

item.name: POST /run — naming a model and a system prompt

request.description:
The whole request body is four fields, and keeping it that way is a decision — the field count on a run endpoint is the clearest measure of whether the runtime still has a boundary.

- `prompt` — required
- `systemPrompt` — replaces the default, does not append to it
- `model` — `<provider>/<model-id>`, or a bare id when exactly one provider serves it. Set the `model` collection variable, or clear it to use the configured fallback
- `thinkingLevel` — `off` | `minimal` | `low` | `medium` | `high`

**Caps are server policy, not request fields.** There is no way to ask for a longer timeout or more turns; if a caller could, the cap would not be one.

Leaving the `model` variable empty is fine — an empty string is treated as "not provided" and the run lands on the configured fallback, so an unfilled template does not become a 400.

Stops a run in flight. 202 if it was running, 404 if no such run is active.

**To use this you need a run that is still going.** Fire the stream request in another tab — its `started` frame sets `runId` immediately — then send this. A JSON run only answers once it is already finished, so cancelling its `runId` correctly 404s.

A cancelled run ends `status: "cancelled"` with **no** `error` field. Cancellation is an outcome, not a fault: the abort pi reports as it unwinds belongs to the reason that won, and a clean cancel should not read as a failure.

item.name: Rejections
item.description: The paths that refuse work. Each has a distinct shape on purpose — 'we are at capacity' and 'your request was malformed' have opposite fixes, and one status code for both would hide which.

request.description:
No `x-agent-key`. Every route except the two health endpoints requires it, compared in constant time.

The process also refuses to boot without `AGENT_S2S_KEY` at all — there is no unauthenticated mode, including in development. This endpoint executes model-authored shell, so a config typo must be a crash loop somebody notices rather than a silently public code-execution endpoint.
Rejected before a single token is spent. A 500 after spending is the wrong default.
The model is resolved against the provider table BEFORE the run is admitted — an unknown model is the caller's mistake and should not occupy one of the concurrency slots while it is discovered.

Not reproducible from a single click — you need more simultaneous runs than `AGENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS` (default 4). Open this in several tabs and fire them together, or:

```
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do (curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} \n" \
  -X POST localhost:8788/run -H 'x-agent-key: devkey' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"prompt":"hi"}' &); done
```

Over the cap the answer is **429, not a queue**. A queue here would be a second scheduler competing with whatever the caller already has, and the caller is better placed to decide whether a rejected run should wait or die.
